Faced with Tomo-chan, Takano-kun was initially frozen stiff.
Worried, I whispered "You're like RoboCop," to which Takano-kun replied in a voice like a robot, "I've forgotten how to walk."
Hearing that, Tomo-chan burst out laughing.
I wonder why just walking through the heat-filled town makes one's mood lift.
It seemed the two of them felt it too, striding along with lively expressions.
Though in Takano-kun's case, I suspect there was another major reason at play.
Every time Tomo-chan spoke to him, he wore a rapt expression as if he were wandering through a field of flowers.
It was so comical that I had to struggle to keep from bursting into laughter.
While browsing secondhand books at a temporary booth set up at the Jinbocho intersection, I bumped into Sabu-san.
He was with his wife, his arms full of more paper bags than he could carry.
His wife was an elegant woman who looked lovely in a kimono; I couldn't help but feel she was a bit too good for him.
And yet, seeing them together, they radiated an unmistakable aura that could only come from decades of shared joy and sorrow.
When I looked at his parcels and said, "You've certainly bought a lot today," his wife nudged him aside and spoke sourly.
"I know, right?
He keeps buying books like this, and now the whole house is overflowing with them.
Perhaps you could come over sometime and buy them all back from us?"
Sabu-san panicked at that. "No, please, anything but that!
I did thin them out just the other day, didn't I?" he pleaded, pressing his hands together in a mock prayer.
We couldn't stop laughing for a while after parting ways with them.
Even as dusk fell, Yasukuni-dori remained crowded, and we walked along it with renewed energy.
We scoured for books to our heart's content.
Tomo-chan led us to a shop called Kintoto Bunko, saying they had interesting things, and there I found elementary school textbooks from the Taisho era for sale.
The archaic language felt surprisingly fresh, and I impulsively spent two thousand yen on a Japanese language textbook.
As night fell and shops began to close, we went to a Western-style restaurant inside Sanseido for dinner.
By then, Takano-kun was quite relaxed, and it seemed he no longer saw imaginary flowers when he looked at Tomo-chan.
He turned out to be incredibly knowledgeable about foreign literature; over dinner, he spoke fluently about the charms of Faulkner, Capote, and Updike, his earlier shyness completely forgotten.
Both Tomo-chan and I were genuinely impressed.
It was an altogether fulfilling and exhilarating day.
Takano-kun thanked me profusely later, but since I was the one who had enjoyed it most, I didn't feel I deserved any gratitude.
On the night of the festival's final day, after closing up the shop, I sat alone in my room, lost in thought.
Looking out the window, the street was so quiet it was hard to believe the week's bustle had even happened.
As I lay on my futon, the ticking of the alarm clock seemed unusually loud.
Staring at the ceiling, I was seized by a strange sense of unease, a loneliness similar to when I first arrived here.
Suddenly, there was a knock at the sliding door, making my shoulders jump.
I looked over timidly and saw an eyeball peering at me through a narrow crack in the door.
"Yikes!"
I let out a scream that would have done a horror movie heroine proud.
"Oh, did I scare you?"
A strangely high-pitched voice said, followed by the appearance of a messy head.
I let out a sigh of relief.

"Don't scare me like that, Uncle!"
"Sorry, sorry."
Carrying large plastic bags in both hands, my uncle asked, "Mind if I come in?"
and stepped into the room.
He pulled out drinks and snacks from the bags, setting them haphazardly on the low table.
There were even potato chips and shredded squid.
"Weren't you going to the festival wrap-up party?"

I asked.
"I just gave my greetings and left.
I wanted to have our own little wrap-up party tonight." He wore a mischievous, boyish smile.
"Come to think of it, we've never actually had a drink together, have we?"
"Oh, that sounds great.
Let's do it!" My earlier gloom vanished instantly, replaced by a bright, light feeling.
As he spread everything out, the room transformed into a modest celebration venue.
We sipped our drinks, listening to the faint chirping of insects through the open window.
Wrapped in the quiet night air, time seemed to slow down, as if the world had stopped turning.
"You seem to have settled into life here quite well, Takako-chan," my uncle said, leaning against the bookshelf and stretching his legs.
"Yeah.

I wasn't sure what to expect at first, but one way or another, I'm really enjoying this holiday from life."
I chuckled as I said it.

"I'm glad to hear that."
"But it's a little frustrating."
"What is?"
"It's like you knew all along.

That I'd end up loving this place."
"That's not true.
I'm just truly happy that you do.

If you want, Takako-chan, you can stay here as long as you like."
Hearing those kind words, my chest tightened with emotion.
"Hey, why are you being so nice to me?

Even though I'm your niece, it's not like we've spent much time together."
"It's because I like you, Takako-chan," he said plainly, without any hint of shyness.
"To you, I might just be some relative you barely know, but to me, it's different.

You're an angel to me."
"An angel?"
I nearly spat out my beer.
No one, man or woman, had ever said something like that to me before.
"That's right, an angel.

And you're my benefactor, too."
"Benefactor?"
I asked, more confused than ever.
As far as I could remember, I'd never done anything for him.
"Yes, my benefactor.

But that's just my own personal feeling. It's probably a boring story, so let's forget it."
"No, I want to hear it," I said, and I meant it.
He looked at me for a moment and asked, "You won't laugh?"
When I nodded, he began to speak slowly, as if reaching back into a distant memory.
"Ever since my late teens, I lived in a state of gloom, unable to find any value in my life. I couldn't fit into my surroundings—school, home—and I just stayed curled up in my own shell.
I was overly self-conscious, with ideals and ambitions to spare, yet I was an empty person who possessed nothing.
That was who I was.

I couldn't imagine for a second that there was a place for me anywhere in this world."
I hadn't had the slightest idea that my uncle had ever felt that way.
But what could that possibly have to do with me being an "angel"?
"It was exactly around that time that my sister gave birth to you.
When she brought you back to the family home to show the grandparents their grandchild, that was when I met you for the first time.
The moment I saw you, so tiny and sleeping soundly wrapped in a blanket, I felt like crying for no reason I could explain.
How should I put it... my heart was just overwhelmed by the mystery of life.
When I thought about how this child would grow up, absorb so many things, and experience so many 'firsts,' I felt as happy as if it were happening to me.
And then, suddenly, I felt my twisted heart being filled with a warm light.
Faintly, I felt a powerful will beginning to sprout within me.
In that moment, I made up my mind.
I would stop hiding in my own rigid cage. I would move, see the world, and learn everything I could from it.
And I would find my own place—a place where I could say with confidence that I belonged.
My travels, my devouring of books—it was all influenced by that.

In short, meeting you was like a revelation given to me."
"A revelation...

That's kind of amazing."
"In a way, you are my benefactor.

That's why I want to do whatever I can for you, Takako-chan."
His tone was so completely earnest that I didn't know how to respond.
I felt childish and ashamed for having felt repulsed and angry at him on my own.
To think that he had thought of me that way all this time...
But I felt like I finally understood why he had been so gentle with me when I was little.
I was such a fool.
Back then, I took his kindness for granted, as if it were my natural right.
Knowing that I had been loved so deeply warmed my heart to its core.
I desperately fought back the tears welling up and said jokingly:

"Uncle, that's not the kind of thing you say while eating shredded squid."
He let out a hearty laugh.
"So, did you finally find your place?"
"Well, I suppose I did.

But it took many long years to get there."
"Is it... could it be here?"
My uncle nodded quietly.
"Yes, right here.
Our little, run-down Morisaki Bookshop.
It's funny, isn't it? To fly out into the world with big ambitions, only to end up right back where I've known every corner of since I was a boy.
But after all that time, I found my way back here.
And by then, I finally understood that it wasn't just a matter of the location.
Right, it's a matter of the heart.
Wherever you are, whomever you're with, if you can be honest with your own heart, then that is your place.
When I realized that, the first half of my life came to an end.
Then I returned to the harbor I loved most and decided to drop anchor there.

To me, this place is sacred, the place where my heart finds the most peace."
"Come to think of it, Sabu-san said a long time ago that you were the savior of this shop..."
"Haha, a savior, huh?
Now that's quite an exaggeration.
Simply put, when my father fell ill and the shop's future was at risk, I just took it over.
At first, my father resisted quite a bit to the idea of me inheriting the shop.
After all, I was a flaky guy, and the used book industry was going through some very tough times.

But I begged him, almost prostrating myself, to let me run this place."
"I see..."
"I mean, how could I just stand by and watch this shop crumble?
This is the place where I spent the most time during my childhood.
I'd sit by my father at the counter, silently reading 'Andersen's Fairy Tales,' and every now and then he'd rub my head with that big hand of his.
I was truly happy in those moments.

I felt that if this place disappeared, all those memories would vanish with it, and I just couldn't bear the thought."
I was completely overwhelmed by my uncle's words.
What was the "uncle" I thought I knew?
This man carried so much human worry and pain inside him.
Wasn't he crying out in his heart far more than I ever was?
His heart was so incredibly rich.
Maybe the way he was always laughing and acting silly in front of others was a poignant effort to keep his true feelings hidden.
But deep inside his chest—
The thought made my heart ache with a deep sadness.
"I wish this place could have been like that for Momoko too...

When she left, I was so desperate to get this shop back on its feet that I never noticed the subtle changes in her heart until it was too late."
"Uncle."
"Hmm?"
"I love this shop.

Very much."
I wanted to say something more clever, but that was all that came out.
Yet, those were my most honest and heartfelt feelings.
"Thank you.
This shop isn't a place that many people need, but as long as there's even one person who feels that way, I feel like I can keep it going for decades to come.

"A boat goes lightly and detachedly, following the current." That's how I want to live alongside this shop."
Saying this, my uncle gave a quiet smile.
Since that night, I began to think more seriously about my own life.
This is a warm and peaceful place, but I can't keep depending on it like this forever.
If I do, I'll never grow.
I'll always be this weak-hearted person. I have to leave.
And I have to start my life over again—
I felt that strongly.
But just as I thought that, a faint-hearted feeling would sprout, and I'd become afraid of leaving.
I want to stay here just a little longer.
That dependent part of me would resurface.

In the end, I just couldn't bring myself to make the break, and I stayed on the second floor of the Morisaki Bookshop for a long time.
I think I was waiting for some kind of sign.
And then, one day, it arrived suddenly.
The phone call came on the second of January.
During the New Year holidays, I didn't return to my parents' home and just stayed on at Morisaki Bookshop.
The shop was closed until the fifth, and my uncle had gone on a hot spring trip with some associates from the union, so I was all alone.
Over the New Year period, Jinbocho was like a deserted city.
Since there aren't many residences nearby, and most restaurants and offices are closed at this time, everyone truly disappears.
Hardly any cars passed along Yasukuni-dori.
On New Year's Eve, I went to Yushima Tenjin with Tomo-chan to pray, but other than that, my schedule was wide open.
So, on New Year's Day and the second, I strolled through the city alone from early morning.
Walking around the hollowed-out city felt wonderful, and even the air seemed much clearer than usual.
I let my scarf flutter in the wind, walking aimlessly, stopping many times to take a deep breath.
When I returned on the evening of the second, the cell phone I'd left in my room was blinking.
Though I had already deleted the contact, I knew immediately who it was from the number in the call log.
Instantly, the good mood I'd been in vanished like a lie, and my chest tightened.
With a trembling finger, I pressed the button and listened to the voicemail.
"Yo, Takako.
It's been a while.
How've you been?
I'm really bored right now, can you come out for a bit?

Call me back and I'll..."
I hit the delete button before the message even finished.

But it was already too late. A feeling of dread spread through my chest with terrifying speed and refused to fade.

Even after the New Year break ended and the shop reopened, the pain in my chest only grew worse.

A cold, heavy, nameless weight began to fill my heart.
I was reminded all over again that I hadn't reached any kind of closure regarding that matter.
I had just tossed it aside, waiting for time to weather the memory away.
But even after six months, just hearing a snippet of his voice made my heart race like this.
I finally understood that as long as I held onto this lingering resentment, nothing would ever be resolved.

"Takako-chan, what are you bottling up inside? If something's wrong, just talk to me."
Toward the end of January, as we were closing up the shop, my uncle suddenly said this, and I was flustered.
"Eh?
How did you know?"
"I can tell just by looking at you.
My eyes aren't just for show, you know," he said with a bit of a pout.
I thought I'd been acting normally so as not to lean on him too much, but it seemed he saw right through everything.
"You'd been looking so much better lately, so I was relieved.
But lately, something's definitely been off.

Even when I talk to you, you're always miles away."
"Was I, I wonder..."
"You were.

Well, I might not be much help, but maybe you'll feel a bit better if you talk about it."
I hadn't intended to tell anyone, but hearing those words from him, I couldn't hold back anymore.
In the end, I had wanted someone to listen.
I had wanted someone to comfort me.
I had wanted to be taken care of.

I felt utterly pathetic, but my defenses crumbled easily at his words.
While we drank together in the room, I poured out everything that had happened to me to my uncle.
Outside, a cold winter rain began to fall, droplets tapping rhythmically against the window.
"It's not really a big deal,"
I began with that disclaimer, and truly, when I actually said it out loud, it didn't seem like much at all.
I had simply lost a boyfriend and lost a job; that was all.
As I talked, I even found myself laughing at how trivial it felt.
Yet, by being open and speaking my mind, I felt somewhat lighter.
My uncle drank whiskey at an unusually fast pace, listening intently without saying a single word.
Even after I spent an hour finishing my story, stumbling and hesitating along the way, he didn't speak for a while.
He just stared at the glass in his hand as if deep in thought.

Finally, he downed his drink and said with resolve:
"Right, let's go make that guy apologize right now!

I was a terrible person.' We'll make him say it with his own mouth."
This unexpected turn of events left me completely stunned.
"Eh?
Right now?
It's already eleven at night, you know?"

"That doesn't matter."
With that, my uncle stood up vigorously and started toward the door.

I hurriedly grabbed his arm.
"It's okay, I was the one being stupid.
I just wanted someone to listen.
Uncle, you're drunk, aren't you?"
"No, I'm not drunk.
Well, actually, I'm a little drunk.
But that doesn't matter.
Aren't you frustrated, Takako-chan?

He just used you for his own convenience."
"Of course I'm frustrated.
I was so, so frustrated, and I still am."
"That's why we're going.
We have to clear away that resentment.

Otherwise, the ghosts of the past will follow you forever."
"But even so, having you show up like a parent in a child's fight would just be embarrassing for me," I said, my voice trembling as if I were about to cry.
"It's not embarrassing at all!"
My uncle let out a shout so loud it was hard to imagine coming from his small frame.
The voice echoed through the tiny room.
"It's not embarrassing.
You are my precious niece.

I really, truly like you, Takako-chan.
So, I can't forgive a guy like that.
This is my ego speaking.

Your uncle just cannot forgive him."
"What you're saying is completely contradictory.
In the end, it's just your own ego, isn't it?"
"Yeah, so I'm going to go clear my head.
Even if you don't go, Takako-chan, I will.
So tell me the address.

I'm going to go punch him a hundred times."
Punch him?
The conversation was heading in a completely outrageous direction.
"Wait, wait, wait.
If you do that, it'll be a disaster.
You'll end up at the police station.
Besides, he played rugby in high school and college, you know?

Uncle Satoru, you're a beanpole—he'll punch you ten thousand times before you get one in."
"I... I won't be intimidated!"
He said it, but I could see his resolve wavering.
"Look, let's just sit down and have another drink," I said with a forced smile, trying to smooth things over.
"Don't run away, Takako-chan," my uncle said, turning to me with a terrifyingly serious tone.
"I'm with you.

So, don't run away."
My uncle stared intently at me with eyes full of strength.
We locked eyes for a few seconds.
Right, if I run away now, nothing will ever change.
I'll be the same person I've always been.
Isn't that obvious?
I bit my lip hard.
"All right.

Let's go, Uncle."
My uncle gave a firm nod.
By the time we arrived in front of his apartment after a forty-minute taxi ride, the rain had become even more intense.
Having brought no umbrella, we ran to the entrance, getting soaked to the bone.
"This is it, right?"
My uncle stopped in front of the door marked Room 204.
"I think so,"
I nodded, digging through my old memories.
Thinking back, I had only visited his place twice while we were dating.
Whenever we met at home, it was always at my place.
I must really be a slow person to only now realize how unnatural that was.
With rain dripping from his hair, my uncle rang the doorbell without a moment's hesitation.
I was shivering all over from the cold and the nerves.
I felt sick to my stomach.

I'd said "all right" with such bravado, but standing before his door, my courage was failing me fast.
How much easier it would be to just leave and pretend none of this happened.
I thought so from the bottom of my heart, staring at the silent iron door.
But it was already too late.
I heard the faint rustle of someone moving on the other side, the sharp click of the lock, and the door opened just a crack.
"Who is it?"
A familiar low voice said.
My uncle immediately grabbed the door and forced it wide open.
Hideaki, dressed in a tracksuit, stood in the entryway with his mouth hanging open in surprise.
He must have just been falling asleep; there were pillow marks on his cheek and his hair was a mess.
But the solid line of his shoulders and those sharp eyes were exactly as I remembered. Well, of course they were—it hadn't been ten years or anything.
Suddenly, a sharp pain shot through my chest.
Hideaki widened his eyes, looked back and forth between us, and then asked my uncle:
"Who the hell are you?"

"I am Takako's uncle."
"Huh?"
"I am Satoru, her uncle.

Her mother is my sister."
"Okay, I get that part, but...
what do you want?"
"Yes, I wouldn't be here if I didn't want something.
Or do we look like we're here to sell you newspaper subscriptions?"
"No, that's what I'm saying.

Tell me why you're here," Hideaki said, his voice tightening with irritation.
I watched their exchange, my heart hammering in my chest.
My uncle was being incredibly provocative tonight.
"The reason we're here is that you did something quite terrible to her.
Surely you can't say you have no idea?"
"Huh?"
The volume of Hideaki's voice went up a notch.
But my uncle didn't flinch.
"You toyed with her, you drove her to quit her job... Do you have no feelings?
Doesn't it make your heart ache to hurt someone that much?"
"Hey, hey, when did I ever hurt her?
Is that what she told you?"

"Yes."
"You're an idiot, aren't you?
I don't care if you're her uncle or whatever, why would you swallow everything she says whole? She's obviously lying.

She was the one who was obsessively pursuing me."
"What benefit would she get from lying?
She quit her job because of you and she's still suffering, you know?"

"She's the one who quit of her own accord, wasn't she?"
Hearing those words, my uncle let out a deep sigh.
"It's no use, Takako-chan.

This man is rotten to the core."
"Hey, old man.

Watch your mouth."
Hideaki stepped forward into the hallway, looming over my uncle.
There was nearly a twenty-centimeter height difference between my small uncle and the tall Hideaki.
My uncle tilted his head back to glare up at him, but he was completely outmatched in terms of presence.
"Is something wrong?"
The person who peeked out from the back of the room in her pajamas was his fiancée, Murano-san.
The worst possible scenario.
I felt so ashamed and utterly exposed standing there; I didn't know what to do with myself.
"Takako-san?"
Murano-san frowned as she recognized me.
"What on earth happened?

You're soaking wet..."
"They just showed up out of nowhere.
Listen, Takako, have you lost your mind?
What were you thinking, barging in at this hour with some old man in tow?"
"Tell him, Takako-chan."
"Um..."
I timidly looked up to find all three of them staring straight at me.
Oh, why did it have to come to this?
Pierced by their collective gaze, I wanted nothing more than to turn into smoke and vanish.
Everyone was waiting in silence for me to speak.
I scrambled through my mind, searching for any words that might smooth things over.
I was just in the neighborhood.
I wanted to get back a book I'd lent you.
I came to say congratulations on your marriage.
No, that's not it.
That's not what I mean.
That's not what I'm supposed to say.
What did I come here for?
I came for closure, didn't I?
If I just gloss over it again now, nothing will ever be resolved.
Steel your resolve, I told myself firmly.

"I..."
Everyone's attention focused on my lips.
I took a deep breath.
My uncle watched over me, his eyes full of encouragement.
Tears threatened to spill over.
At the same time, all the emotions that had been trapped at the bottom of my heart for so long came rushing up.
Before I could even think, a flood of words suddenly poured out of my mouth.
"I came because I wanted you to apologize!
To you, it might have been just a bit of fun, but for me, it was everything!
I really, truly loved you!
I'm a human being, too, I have feelings!
I might have just seemed like a convenient woman to you, but I think, I breathe, and I cry just like anyone else!
Do you have any idea how much you hurt me?

I... I..."
After that, the words wouldn't come.
Drenched with rain and tears, I was a complete and utter mess.
But after six months, I had finally been able to say what I'd wanted to say at the restaurant that night.

"Well said, Takako-chan,"
my uncle said, pulling my shoulder close to him.
"Now, what will you do?
She told you exactly how she feels.

You have to respond to that properly."
Hideaki looked down and remained silent for a long time, before finally muttering softly.
"This is ridiculous.
I don't have time to deal with people who have nothing better to do than this.
I'm going to bed.

If you don't want me to call the police, just go home already."
With that, he quietly closed the door.
The click of the lock turning inside echoed through the silent hallway.
"Hey, you coward!"
My uncle lunged at the door like a bull and started pounding on it with his fists. I desperately grabbed him from behind.

"It's enough, Uncle."
"But, Takako-chan..."
"It's really okay now.
I feel much better.
I feel so incredibly relieved—more than I ever have in my life.

That might be the first time I've ever actually shouted my feelings at someone."
I said that and gave my uncle a wide, messy grin, my face a map of tears and rain.
"If you say so, Takako-chan..." my uncle muttered, looking only half-convinced.
"Are you sure?"
"Yes.
Come on, let's go home.

We'll both catch our death if we stay out here."
"...All right."
"Yeah."
I whispered a final "Goodbye" in my heart toward the door and walked away.
We hardly spoke in the taxi on the way back.
My uncle leaned back in the seat as if he'd exhausted all his strength, and I sat beside him, released from the tension and lost in my own thoughts.
Hideaki wasn't the only one at fault.
I had known that from the beginning.
Half of the responsibility for how things turned out lay with me.

It was the result of my own carelessness and lack of will.
However, I just had to say what I felt.
No matter how selfish it might seem, I needed to convey what was on my mind.
I had been suffering all this time from my own weakness, from the fact that I hadn't been able to speak up.
It might have been an unfair blow to Hideaki, who clearly had no sense of guilt, but I absolutely needed to vent those feelings.
Otherwise, I couldn't move forward.
I would never have been able to take that next step.
If my uncle hadn't given me that push, I would have been stuck with these feelings forever.
I tried to find the words to thank my uncle, turning them over and over in my head.
But nothing seemed quite right.
In the end, only one phrase surfaced.
So, I just said it, simply and honestly.

"Thank you..."
My uncle smiled and pulled my shoulder toward him.
Feeling the warmth of his body, I let out a sigh of deep relief. I wasn't alone.
Yes, there was someone who worried about me like this and got angry on my behalf.
Until just recently, I felt like I was all alone in this vast world, yet someone so close was looking out for me.
That thought filled me with an indescribable joy.
The taxi drove quietly through the rain-soaked streets where neon lights blurred in the mist.
It was shortly after that I decided to leave the shop.
Strange as it was, that event gave me the momentum I needed.
The weight I'd been carrying had vanished, and I finally felt light enough to move on.
I found a new room and was set to move in March.
It was quite far from the shop, but that couldn't be helped.
There was still so much uncertainty about my future, but through a connection from my old job, I managed to get a part-time position at a small design firm.
When I told him I was leaving, my uncle was stunned. "You don't have to decide so suddenly..." he said, clearly flustered.
But I had already made up my mind.
"I've enjoyed my long vacation from life for quite a while now.

If I don't set out to find my own place soon, I'll end up gaining nothing."
After hearing that, my uncle said no more.
During my final month at the Morisaki Bookshop, I savored every moment.
I put my heart into my work and read as much as I could.
I gave the shop and the upstairs room a thorough cleaning as a gesture of gratitude.

I even went back to the room where I'd haphazardly piled the books on my first day and organized them with care.
I told the regulars and the staff at Suboru that I was leaving.
Everyone seemed so genuinely sad to see me go that it almost made me cry, realizing how much I'd come to be cared for.
Sabu-san even joked, "Come and marry my son," and seemed half-serious about setting us up.
Takano-kun and Tomo-chan even threw a small farewell party for me.
We shared a hot pot on the second floor of the shop and hung out late into the night.
Tomo-chan was genuinely sad to lose her reading companion. "Let's go to the festival together again next year," she promised.
Takano-kun told me in confidence that he had recently taken Tomo-chan to a movie in Shibuya.
They weren't quite dating yet, but for someone as shy as him, it was massive progress.
I felt a surge of joy for him and shouted, "That's great!"
and couldn't help but give his thin back a hearty slap.
Later, I unexpectedly heard from Hideaki's fiancée, Murano-san, and we met at a cafe to talk.
What weighed on me most was that I had caused her so much trouble that night.
I went to our meeting fully prepared to apologize as profusely as I could.
However, as soon as we sat down, she was the one who gave me a deep, sincere bow.
She had been suspicious of his behavior for a while, and my presence that night had confirmed her fears. She had questioned him until he finally confessed everything.
She told me she had never even dreamed that I was the one he'd been seeing until that night.
Murano-san apologized over and over, and even when I told her I was also to blame, she just kept shaking her head.
She had decided to call off the wedding entirely.

When I tried to apologize again, she stopped me. "It's not your fault, Takako-san," she said firmly.
I still felt a lingering sense of guilt, but when I told my uncle about it later, he just said, "She's doing the right thing.
Better to find out what a loser he is now than after they're married."

It was a typical response for someone who despised Hideaki as much as my uncle did, but I had to admit there was some truth to it. I felt a weight lift from my shoulders.

On my last night at the shop, my uncle and I sat on the second-floor balcony, drinking coffee and gazing up at the winter sky.
As a parting gift, he gave me a massive stack of secondhand books.
He said they were all stories that had deeply moved him when he was young.
Peering into the heavy paper bag, I saw it was filled with works by authors I'd come to appreciate, like Takehiko Fukunaga and Kazuo Ozaki.
We spent that final night in a state of quiet, comfortable ease.
And I know I will never forget the words he said to me then.
He started by saying, "There's one thing I want you to promise me," and then he said this:
"Don't ever be afraid to love people.
While you're still young, I want you to love as many people as you can.
Even if it ends in sadness, please don't live a life where you never love anyone. That's a lonely way to be.
I was so worried that this experience would make you close yourself off to love forever.
Loving someone is a beautiful thing.
Please, never forget that.
The memory of loving someone never truly leaves you.
It stays with you, keeping your heart warm for the rest of your life.

When you get to be my age, you'll understand what I mean."
He looked at me and asked, "So, can you promise me that?"
he asked.
"I understand.
I promise," I said, nodding.
"I think I've already learned that here, thanks to you.

So you don't need to worry about me."
"I see.

Then I know you'll be just fine, wherever you go."
"Yeah.

Thank you, Uncle."

On the morning I left, I stood in the early morning sunlight and took one last long look at the Morisaki Bookshop.
It was just a small, old wooden building.
It felt almost impossible to believe that I had actually lived there.
I stood there for a long time, my breath blooming white in the air. The street was bathed in soft morning light.
None of the shops were open yet, and the air was filled with a quiet, indescribable peace.
I straightened my posture and gave a deep, formal bow toward the shop.
I vowed to never forget the lessons I'd learned during my time at the Morisaki Bookshop.
I also gave my sincere thanks to my uncle, who had come out so early to see me off.
He had become such a massive presence in my life.
It was strange to think that when I first arrived, I could never have imagined feeling this way.
When it came time to say goodbye, his tough act from the night before vanished completely, and he started sobbing like a child.
"I've changed my mind, I don't want you to go!

Don't leave me, Takako-chan!"
He gripped my hand tightly and wouldn't let go.
"I'll come visit you all the time," I said, comforting him, even though it felt like our roles were reversed.
"So please, take care of yourself.

And keep this shop safe for me."
I knew that if I stayed even a second longer, my own resolve would crumble.
So I quickly said my final goodbye and started walking down the street.
I marched all the way to the end of Sakura-dori without looking back once.
As I walked, the memories flooded my heart, and tears began to sting my eyes.

But I fought them back until I reached the end of the road.
I had a sudden premonition and stopped, slowly turning around.
There was my uncle, a small figure in the distance, standing in the middle of the road and waving frantically.
Seeing him like that, I couldn't hold it in anymore.
The tears came pouring out, uncontrollably.
With my face crumpled and wet with tears, I waved back with all my might.
He responded by waving even harder.
The morning sun was shining brightly behind him.
"Take care of yourself!" I shouted.
I turned on my heel and began walking down Yasukuni-dori, which was already starting to fill with people.
The people passing by probably thought I was a strange woman, walking along and sobbing like that.
But I didn't care at all.
Because I was crying because I wanted to, and these were the happiest tears I had ever shed in my life.
In the crisp early morning air, there was the faintest hint of spring.
And I walked straight ahead into it, without looking back.
